maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY    INCREASE IN INITIAL PRICE OF WHEAT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY    INCREASE IN INITIAL PRICE OF WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement to the house with regard to the marketing of western wheat, oats and barley. As hon. members of the house know, phenomenal grain crops were produced in the prairie provinces last year: a record wheat crop of 664 million bushels, a record barley crop of 281 million bushels and a large oats crop of 346 million bushels. The marketing of grain production of this magnitude has of course presented many difficulties and it was realized early in the crop year that these problems could be met only through aggressive selling on the part of the Canadian wheat board and the provision of maximum transportation for the movement of grain.
I am happy to report that good progress is being made with the receiving and the merchandising of western grains. In spite of elevator congestion, which must be
expected in the face of the size of the 1952 grain crops, producers had delivered a total of 461 million bushels of grain up to February 5,	1953-a quantity of grain not
exceeded during the corresponding period in any of the past ten years. As grain is moved forward from country elevators, producers will continue to add to their deliveries of grain throughout the crop year.
The bumper crops of 1952 have been accompanied by an excellent demand particularly for wheat and barley. Exports of grain are running well ahead of the corresponding period a year ago when new records were established. I have every reason to believe that the record exports of 1951-52 will be exceeded by a substantial margin by exports in 1952-53. The Canadian wheat board has made very large sales so far in the crop year and has large sales on its books for delivery during the balance of the crop year.
Having regard to the present sales position, the government has approved an increase in the initial price of all grades of wheat, excepting durums, from $1.40 per bushel to $1.60 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern in store Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver. The increase will become effective on March 2, 1953. This means that an adjustment payment of 20 cents per bushel will be made to producers covering their deliveries of all grades of wheat other than durums to the board between August 1, 1952, and February 28, 1953.
In the case of durum wheat, there has been an exceptionally strong demand during the present crop year and actually the production of durum wheat is not now sufficient to meet the demand for this type of grain. Therefore, the initial prices of all grades of durum wheat will be increased by 25 cents per bushel and an adjustment payment in this amount will be made to all producers delivering durum wheat to the board between August 1,	1952, and February 28, 1953.
This will bring the initial prices of durum grades from their present level of $1.40 per bushel for No. 1 amber durum in store Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver to $1.65 per bushel effective on March 2, 1953. There appears to be a growing market for durum varieties of wheat and it is my hope that this increase in the initial payment for this variety of wheat will serve to encourage additional durum production in 1953.

Grain
In regard to coarse grains, we must recognize that 1952 production and estimated marketings of oats and barley during the crop year 1952-53 involve extraordinary quantities. From the 1952 production, it is estimated that producers will have surpluses of about 175 million bushels of each grain. The position in respect to barley is satisfactory in respect to both marketing and sales and accordingly the government is increasing the initial price of all grades of barley by 15 cents per bushel effective March 2, 1953. The new initial price of barley will be $1.11 per bushel basis No. 3 CW 6 row barley in store Fort William or Port Arthur as compared with the present initial price of 96 cents per bushel. This will involve an adjustment payment of 15 cents per bushel on all grades of barley delivered to the board between August 1,	1952, and February
28, 1953.
I now wish to deal with the oats position. Up to the present time only about one-third of possible deliveries of oats for the crop year have been delivered by producers and while sales have been satisfactory, the Canadian wheat board do not feel in a position to make a definite recommendation at this time in regard to an increase in the initial price for oats. You will recall that a similar position was taken a year ago in regard to oats. Accordingly, it is the policy of the government to leave the initial price of oats at its present level for the balance of the crop year.
The adjustment payments which I have mentioned are, of course, subject to the one per cent levy under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
The wheat adjustment payment will commence on April 1 and will be followed immediately by the barley adjustment payment. If the present rate of producers' deliveries continues until the end of February, the adjustment payments on wheat and barley will amount to about $80 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: PROVISION IN SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES WITH RESPECT TO EDUCATION OF NEWCOMERS
speechtext:
Hon. members will be interested to know that it is the intention of the government to provide in the supplementary estimates for a sum from which grants may be made to provincial governments with respect to the education of our newcomers in citizenship. It is a well recognized fact that the sooner the newcomers are made familiar with the English or the French language, the habits and customs of the Canadian people, our history, our form of government, and our democratic processes, the sooner they will become useful and productive citizens. There are at the moment

approximately 45,000 adult newcomers attending citizenship classes in the various provinces and we hope that these classes will be continued and increased in number.
The grant to each provincial government would be one-half the amount contributed by the provincial government for these citizenship classes. Letters are going forward to each provincial premier advising him of this and inviting his government to join in making a suitable agreement.

speechtext:
1.	Is the ordinary type of army boot, generally designated "boots, ankle" equipped with steel -lcats on toe and heel, the type of boot on issue to troops in Korea?
2.	If so, has this type of boot been found suitable in Korea?
3. If a change was made in the type of boot issued, what was the date of this change, what was the new type of boot issued, and what proportion of the personnel in the Korean brigade was issued with a different type?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
1.	Boots generally issued to the 25th Canadian infantry brigade in Korea are the regular type of boot known as "boots ankle" issued to Canadian forces in Canada and Europe. These boots are about 7J inches high; they have steel plates on the toes and heels and are hobnailed as necessary. Tank crews are issued with "boots ankle CAC", which are similar to the regular "boots ankle" except that the soles and heels are rubber and not equipped with steel plates or hob nails. Both knee and hip length rubber boots are issued for special purposes. During 1951-52 about 50 per cent of the brigade were issued with "boots rubber soles leather uppers" similar to the shoepacs used by lumbermen, being about 12J inches high. On balance this boot was not found to be generally satisfactory for
use in Korea because of the conditions of climate and terrain found there. A number of British boots "cold-wet-weather" were purchased and issued. Also, some 1,500 pairs of boots "X-49-C" made in Canada were issued for trial purposes in 1951-52. These boots are similar to the "boots ankle" except that composition soles and heels were used in the design. The results of these trials are now being evaluated. A further 500 pair of boots were issued for trials in Korea in June, 1952. These boots are similar to the X-49-C boots, but with a leather extension 3f inches high, making the total height of the boot about 11 inches. Other user trials have been made of other boots of Canadian, British and United States design and these trials are continuing.
2.	So far the Canadian ankle boot, as modified with the leather extension, has been found a most satisfactory boot for general use in Korea. A substantial number of the regular boots ankle have been modified in a similar way in the theatre. As stated in answer to question 1, other types of footwear have been, and are being given user trials.
3.	See answers to Nos. 1 and 2.

That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, 1944, to extend its operation for a further period by closing out on March 31, 1953, in lieu of February 28, 1954, the present three year pool of loans guaranteed by the government under the act and by providing for a new three year pool commencing April 1, 1953, and ending March 31, 1956; to provide further that the maximum amount of bank loans made in the new period and guaranteed under the act shall be three hundred million dollars.

In looking over the list here I find that in 1949 not one loan was made in Newfoundland under this act. I believe that the only publicity that has been given the act in Newfoundland is the publicity that I have given it. I have been trying to tell the people there of the benefits they can get under this legislation. But they were up against the fact that the bankers themselves were not familiar with the legislation and shied clear of it. If you look at the figures, you will see that it was not until last year that any substantial amount was loaned.
Since January 1, 1951, there have been thirty-three loans made in Newfoundland. Thirty of them were in 1952. In 1950 there were only two loans of less than $1,000. It seems to me that someone is slipping up there. There is not much good in having legislation for the benefit of two or three provinces. Every province should receive the benefit of it. Inasmuch as Newfoundland has come into confederation and the people of Newfoundland have not received the benefit of the publicity that the people of western Canada get, it seems to me that some special effort should be made to draw these things to their attention.
I have in my hand several of the booklets that have been issued by the Department of Finance. One is entitled "Your Invisible Farmhand". It is an illustrated booklet showing farmers how they can get assistance to improve their homes. Another is entitled "What the Western Dailies Say About the Farm Improvement Loans Act". It contains extracts from different papers in the prairie provinces in 1945 praising this legislation. Then there is one entitled "Farm Improvement Loans". I should like to know if the parliamentary assistant is in a position to tell me how much of this literature has been circulated in Newfoundland. What efforts

Quite a few pamphlets outlining the advantages of the act have been published by the Department of Finance. They are available at the request of bank managers all over the country. The head offices of the banks see to it that their branches get the publicity. I do not know how it is in Newfoundland. These pamphlets are at the disposal of the bank managers and the farmers themselves. According to my information the best publicity has been given-I will take my own constituency, if you wish, where the number of loans increased sharply in the last years-by dealers in farm implements, farm tractors and so on, who have convinced their clients that it is a very good way to obtain credit to pay for farm implements, trucks and tractors.
The hon. member is surprised that there has not been a larger amount of loans in Newfoundland. We must not forget that according to the 1951 census there are only 3,626 farms in Newfoundland, and out of that total 2,840 are operated by part-time farmers or are farms where the value of the products sold is less than $250 a year. Of the balance of 786 farms, 583 are such that the value of the products sold is less than $2,500 a year. That leaves in the whole of Newfoundland only 203 farms, the products of which sold for more than $2,500 in 1951.
I have never had the advantage of visiting Newfoundland but I understand that the principal occupation there is fishing. I understand that many fishermen have small pieces of land and are part-time farmers, but their main occupation is not farming. Therefore when you take into account the fact that there are only slightly over 200 farms which yield an income of more than $2,500 a year, it is not surprising that the amount and the number of loans have been so low.

speechtext:
Just on that point, I think it follows from the nature and purpose of the act that, particularly in western Canada, the greatest benefit of this measure would come from the financing of farm machinery. This is exactly the way the development has occurred in the west. I want to take this opportunity of joining with others to say that, in my estimation, this scheme is the best one ever devised in a great many years. It has had a great effect on agriculture throughout the western provinces. This measure has contributed to the peace of mind of the farmers, and has contributed greatly to the security of the farmers.
I believe it would be fair to say that this legislation, was devised primarily for the purpose of assisting farmers in securing machinery and equipment. It will be recalled that some years ago there was an investigation into the cost of farm machinery. Before this measure came into being the implement companies had to have their own credit organizations. There were a number of collectors attached to these organizations, who had to go throughout the country visiting the farmers individually before the crop was harvested to make sure when it would be harvested. Then, a second trip was necessary when the crop was harvested so the collector would be the first one to get the money. Really, these people were chasing the farmers up and down the country continuously. Naturally this was a costly procedure for them, and they had to charge from 7 per cent to 12 per cent interest, on the money that they were advancing to the farmer to purchase machinery. This proved to be a costly operation for the farmer.
Now, when this system came into being the farmer was able to go to the bank and secure a loan at 5 per cent. He could pay cash for the farm implements, so that from then on he had nothing more to do with the equipment company. When he sold his grain he got his money, went to the bank, and paid what he owed the bank and that was the end of it. In this respect, the act has been of great benefit to the farmers. In passing, I might say that I feel this measure is a living memorial to the late Dr. Clark. I think it is to the credit of this ' government as well that they had the vision to recognize the merit of this proposition, . and the courage to put it into force.

It is obvious that in western Canada the main purpose of this act is to enable loans to be secured for farm implements. In the last annual report for which we have complete figures, we find that 92 per cent of the money lent under this act was for financing the purchase of farm implements, and this amounted to $78 million. It is interesting to note that this $78 million represented a credit of $137 million in farm equipment. As the parliamentary assistant pointed out last night, it is estimated that that represents 45 per cent of all the new farm trucks purchased and 60 per cent of all the new combines purchased, so that one can see that the act has a great bearing on financing in western Canada.
At this point I should like to say something about the risk in agriculture. For some years past farmers have not been considered a good risk. I believe that this report provides a glowing tribute to the farmer, and shows clearly that he has been careful about his debts. It shows he has been faithful to his obligations. During the first year of operation there were no losses to the government at all. During the second and third years there were no losses to the country. During the last complete year for which we have figures, 1951, there were eighteen claims made on the government totalling about $6,000; that is eighteen claims out of 75,000 loans and $6,000 claimed out of $85 million lent. It is interesting to note that since the inception of the act there have been 54 claims out of 248,000 loans, with a loss to the government of $26,000 out of a total of $255 million lent. You can see that this measure has cost the country very little and has unlocked a great source of credit.
As we have seen, in the case of farm machinery, the loans of $78 million represented $137 million, so that by the same token it could almost be said that for this slight cost we have put practically a half billion dollars at the disposal of agriculture.
I just want to say a word on the question raised by the hon. member for Souris; I refer to the question of increasing the maximum of $3,000. As the parliamentary assistant has pointed out, there does not appear to be great pressure to have the $3,000 increased. According to the figures tabled, for instance those in Manitoba who have availed themselves of the total loan of $3,000 since the inception of the act amount to approximately 700 out of a total of 44,000. There therefore does not seem to be great pressure on the ceiling. Personally I must confess that I have never had any demands for it, and I do not know of any farm organization which
Farm Improvement Loans Act has raised the question. There may be a case for it but at the present time I am not aware of it.
But there is one thing that I think we should not lose track of and about which we should be careful in our consideration of this act. We have a good act. We have one that is doing a wonderful job and is serving a definite purpose. I think we should be careful not to attempt to stretch it to do something it was not meant to do. For instance, it was never meant to replace what the Canadian Farm Loan Act, for instance, has been set up to do. These two pieces of legislation should be made to go together and to supplement one another. We should be careful that we do not do anything whereby one will supersede the other.
As I said, the act as it is now has been most successful. It has done a wonderful job. There may be a case for increasing the ceiling, but I do not think there is a great case for it at the moment. Before we increase the ceiling my suggestion is that we be extremely careful that we do not weaken the act by attempting to make it do too much. It was made to do a job, and it is doing it. Let us be sure that we keep it that way.

I understand. That is now clear. But the criticism which we in this group have of the legislation is that we still feel even when it is passed, and even with the existence of the Canadian farm loan board and everything else, it still falls short of meeting the credit needs of Canadian agriculture. We still think that many farmers are not going to be able to get the credit they need. We suggest that there are several steps which could be taken to strengthen this legislation.
As every hon. member knows, in recent years there has been a drift of farmers away from the farms into the city. That situation has been caused by a number of factors. One of the main ones is that young farmers are finding it harder and harder to get together adequate capital with which to finance farm operations. If they are young farmers starting out, they find that the price of land is extremely high; the price of machinery has skyrocketed; the price of livestock is out of reach. If they are established farmers and want to expand their operations they find it extremely difficult to get capital.
We think there are three or four steps that could be taken to make this legislation more effective. In the first place, I cannot agree with the hon. member for Provencher when he says that the ceiling on loans should not be increased. We think that the ceiling should be increased from $3,000 to at least $6,000. After all, if you buy a tractor out west today, it costs more than $3,000. One hon. member pointed out last night, I think, that a combine costs about $6,000. Therefore the present ceiling in the act is not practical as far as western farmers are concerned.
The second proposal we would suggest is that the banks lending under the provisions of this act be more liberal. We think they should be more generous in making loans. Quite frequently today farmers who really need money cannot get it. The banks lend money under orthodox banking principles and frequently marginal farmers are considered to be too great a risk. Even where the farmer is a good risk we quite frequently find that the banks will not lend the full $3,000. I think evidence of that fact was given last night by the parliamentary assistant.

I think the third step which could be taken under this act is for down payments to be lowered. Down payments on agricultural equipment now are 33J per cent. Perhaps they could be reduced to 20 per cent. On home and building repairs the down payment is 20 per cent. I think possibly that could be reduced to 10 per cent. The time limit of seven years is fairly short if we are going to increase the amount of the loan. Possibly that limit should be extended to ten years.
I suggest that amendments of this kind would not cost the taxpayer any money or, at worst, a very small amount. After all, total losses under the act have been $36,000 in eight years. That is less than $5,000 a year. I therefore believe that we could bring in reforms of this kind, and do it without their costing the taxpayers any additional sums of money. As I say, the main purpose of this act is to create better credit facilities for farmers. Today we have not those credit facilities and we are not going to have them unless the government steps into the field. I suggest that agriculture is far too important in this country to be restricted as it is today by lack of credit.

I should like to say I am glad to support the measure. We think the legislation has provided a very valuable service to farmers. I think it represents the culmination of demands by farm organizations to have a low rate of interest and in order that the capital borrowed may be repaid over a longer period of time.
Before this legislation came down the banks used to make money available to farmers at 8 per cent, but they lent it for a period of three months only, which would be extended at the end of that period. But it became evident that loans to farmers have to be made over a longer period than three months or six months to meet their needs. This I believe provides for a period of two years, with 30 per cent paid down by the farmer when the machine is bought, and another 30 per cent has to be paid in the fall and the next 30 per cent the year after.
I would agree that in many cases it would help if the ceiling were raised, and also if the period of the payment could be extended. But I notice that the parliamentary assistant points out that it is really not necessary to raise the ceiling because only a very small percentage of the farmers are borrowing up to that amount. Farm Improvement Loans Act that the banks will not lend more, but in the area that I represent that is not the case. That is the trouble; and therefore if they do not have so much cash they have to borrow less in order to pay down 30 per cent. That is the reason in many instances why the farmers are not borrowing more under this legislation.
I will admit that in many cases that has been got around by the machine companies accepting the trade-in as the first payment. They have been very good in doing that. I think it is well advertised in my constituency, and it is very generally used for the purchase of farm machinery and such things. It is pretty well administered, because it is administered by the chartered banks.

Our farmers are in a hazardous occupation. There is no stability in their markets, and they do not like to risk too much; therefore I do not think I would press for an increase in the amount that may be borrowed. However, if it was going to benefit the farmers in other places, then I can see no particular risk in increasing the ceiling, because the governor in council and the banks have put adequate limitations in the regulations which require security that would protect the loan up to $5,000 just as it does up to $3,000.

This brings me back again to my province, and I think this is something which is worthy of the attention of this parliament. We are affected in many ways. We have two classes of farmers. They are all farmers, and they depend entirely on farming, but we have a farmer who has a small income. He is working hard to get it. He is eking out a living. That man cannot go into the bank and give a statement which indicates that he can pay back a loan of $400 or $500 for certain within a year or two.
Then we have the other man who is a larger farmer, he grows potatoes mainly. He is in a different position, because as I said once before in this house, it seems that the policy is driving our people into two classes. The rich are doing better but the poor are getting poorer. The other class of farmer does not need to use this act so much because he can finance himself. A good farmer can go to his bank and borrow on bonds-a good many of them might have them-and he can borrow at less than 5 per cent. Therefore as a matter of business he does not use this legislation.

The other man who may need it to get some farm machinery cannot satisfy the bank that he can grow sufficient crops and market them at a profit sufficiently high to repay that loan within three or four years. I am not blaming the act; I think it only fair, from what has been said here this afternoon, to say that in my particular part of the province this act is well known. It has been well advertised, and it is utilized by those who can use it. It is a good thing. I am very much in favour of extending it. I would support raising the ceiling, because I believe it is in good hands. Even if the ceiling is raised it may not assist many down in my part of the dominion, but it might assist other people in the dominion. It might assist some farmers, and if so I do not see that the government will lose anything on it because it is in the hands of the banks and the banks are good administrators of this type of business.
Therefore I am not going to take up more time on this matter, except to say that I am willing to support it as it is, and I would be quite willing to support it if the ceiling were raised.

Mr. Chairman, before the resolution carries I should like to say a word or two in respect to this measure. I want to congratulate the government on expanding the amount of money to be available for loans of this kind, but I also want to draw attention to the general idea which has been advanced by the hon. member for Assiniboia. There are many large farms in my constituency, and I find that a good many farmers there feel unhappy because no provision is made to assist young men establishing themselves on farms.
As the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out, it costs at least $20,000 to set up a farm in these areas where the size ranges from half a section to probably two and a half sections. With that amount being required it is sometimes impossible to devise any means whereby young men can get started. The result is that we lose a great number of our young men who would be admirable farmers, who have the skill and desire for farming, just because they cannot get established.
I would say that is exceedingly bad business for the country. We want the finest of our young men to stay in Canada. We want our young men on farms where they can support themselves and raise Canadians for the future. If we lose them to the United States or to the cities where they undertake work which may not be permanent, we suffer a serious loss.
There is a general feeling in my constituency that the maximum is far too low, which would naturally follow from what I have just said. I am not prepared to say that this is the particular measure under which provision should be made for larger loans, but I do submit that the government should keep that in mind and devise a scheme before too long to take care of the situation which I have just pointed out.
The interest rate is far too high. Five per cent is unnecessary. I should like to draw the attention of the house once more to the fact that the Bank of Canada can create money today by just printing on paper without having any gold backing whatever. We passed a measure last year making it possible to do that on the basis of bonds. It is simply ridiculous, it is a reflection upon the intelligence of the people in this house to expect our young people or even our older people to pay 5 per cent interest on money which the Bank of Canada can run off just as rapidly as it can print it.

We should remember what can be done under the Bank of Canada Act. On pages 140 and 141 of "The Canadian Banking System" by Professor James Holladay-I am sure I am right -it is pointed out that the Bank of Canada working in conjunction with Canadian chartered banks can take one dollar gold and upon that dollar of gold, establish $84 of currency and credit in Canada. I do not intend to enter into a discussion of finance, but the fact is that under this measure we are charging 5 per cent interest on money. I say that is simply not in accordance with common sense under the financial system we have at the present time. I maintain that the interest rate is far too high.
I am not saying that the banks should be called upon to lend money at a rate lower than 5 per cent, but I am saying that it ought to be possible for the federal government through the instruments which it has at its disposal to grant assistance to the banks, to subsidize them, so that they can lend at 3 per cent. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that where an emergency of an apprehended war faces a democratic government, that has on its statute books an act like the War Measures Act, the proper course for that democratic government is to come to parliament and ask it to give certain specified emergency powers, under proper precautions as to the tabling of the orders in council and proper precautions as to the control that parliament will have over all the acts done under those emergency powers. And I say that it is quite reasonable that that special act should remain upon the statute books during the continuation of such emergency, rather than that the government and parliament should have to fall back upon the much wider powers of the War Measures Act.
